{"path":"/GitHub/link_6a1a5af1b40c8191affccbb98ac60fa3/create_blob","args":{"repository_full_name":"Satobloc/HsH","content":"# Whirligig / Analemma: terminology and functional reconstruction\n\n**Date:** 2026-10-21. **Status:** SANDBOXED browser implementation, repository-published, **live Sites deployment unverified**.\n\n## Direct user correction and provenance\n\nThe early records' **GrAnn / Great Annulum** was a mistaken term. The user intended an **Analemma**. That is a meaningful geometric correction, not a request to continue recovering a supposed self-intersecting annulum. Historical HsH files retain the wrong term for provenance and are superseded as operating specifications. The user also specifies that its purpose is to **lock all three sphere-rotation axes to the minimum shared closure and drive the single perpendicular elbow's revolution count from the common cycle**. The sphere is to roll on the **inner radial torus surface**.\n\nFor astronomical context only, the conventional solar analemma is the figure-eight locus of apparent solar declination versus equation of time at a fixed mean time of day. See the US Naval Observatory's [Equation of Time](https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/eqtime) explanation. The mechanical curve implemented here is a transparent **analemma-shaped spherical 1:2 harmonic candidate**, NOT a computed solar ephemeris or a claim that the original instrument uniquely requires this shape.\n\n## Implemented 3D material contact curve\n\nLet \\(t\\in[0,2\\pi]\\) run over one material Analemma circuit and \\(A>0\\) control its spherical aperture:\n\n\\[\nG_A(t)=\\frac{(-1,\\ A\\sin t,\\ A(\\sin2t+0.27\\sin t))}{\\|(-1,\\ A\\sin t,\\ A(\\sin2t+0.27\\sin t))\\|}.\n\\]\n\nThis is a closed self-intersecting curve on the **unit sphere** with unequal lobes. \\(G_A(0)=G_A(\\pi)=(-1,0,0)\\), but the two branches have distinct tangent directions. Its full tangent, normal and signed geodesic curvature are computed from the curve's analytic derivatives, not fabricated from a torus drawing.\n\nThe older reconstruction's circular carrier has been replaced in both world and sphere-body displays. The UI labels it **Analemma**. Internal legacy variable names and research filenames may retain `grann` for implementation compatibility, but should not be mistaken for the user's corrected terminology.\n\n## Inner-torus rolling and minimum return\n\nLet the torus major radius be \\(R\\), both sphere radius and torus tube radius be \\(b=a\\), and \\(\\psi\\) parameterize the torus-centerline orbit. Define unit radial \\(e_r\\), orbital tangent \\(e_\\phi\\), vertical \\(e_z\\).\n\nThe selected point on the **inner** torus wall is \\(Donomphulon=(R-b)e_r\\). The separately named **outer** radial point remains \\(P_{ivot}=(R+b)e_r\\). Sphere center \\(C=Re_r\\). The selected contact offset is \\(-b e_r\\).\n\nNo-slip at this nominated inner contact:\n\\[\n\\dot C+\\omega\\times(-b e_r)=0.\n\\]\n\nFor the material Analemma, let \\(s\\) be **actual spherical arc length**, \\(g=G_A(s)\\), \\(t=dg/ds\\), \\(h=g\\times t\\), and \\(\\kappa_g\\) be signed geodesic curvature. The SO(3) lock is\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal Q(\\psi)=[-e_r,\\ e_\\phi,\\ -e_z]\\,[g,t,h]^T,\\qquad\n\\frac{ds}{d\\psi}=\\frac{R}{b}-1.\n\\]\n\nThis produces\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\frac{\\omega}{\\dot\\psi}=\\frac{R}{b}e_z+\n\\left(\\frac{R}{b}-1\\right)\\kappa_g(s)e_r}.\n\\]\n\nThe required \\(+z\\) rolling spin now has the **same sign as orbital travel**, unlike the earlier incorrect outer-wall model. The radial spin component rotates through **x and y** as the sphere goes around the torus, so all three spatial axes participate. This is mathematically an **inner selected-contact** constraint, not global no-slip over the nonisolated \\(b=a\\) contact locus.\n\nLet \\(L_G(A)\\) be the true spherical arclength of one material Analemma. One torus orbit moves through \\(2\\pi(R/b-1)\\) of material arc length. The model searches for the **smallest positive even** winding count \\(n\\), subject to its openly stated admissible aperture \\(0<A\\le2\\), satisfying\n\n\\[\nn L_G(A)=2\\pi\\left(\\frac{R}{b}-1\\right).\n\\]\n\nWith \\(R=1.65\\), \\(b=0.55\\), the minimum is \\(n=2\\), numerical \\(A\\approx0.935206924\\), and \\(L_G\\approx2\\pi\\). This is *minimal within this declared family and bounded aperture*, not a universal minimum across all possible analemmas.\n\nThe R/Q moving sweep plane still intersects each source curve separately. The one and only perpendicular elbow is phase-locked to \\(\\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)\\), where \\(m\\) is the chosen integer R/Q sweep count per torus orbit. No extra projector and no independent elbow-turn slider.\n\n### Numerical transport detail\n\nThe current browser integrates Analemma arclength with composite Simpson quadrature, inverts its monotone \\(s(t)\\) table with a bracket and a local Newton/Simpson refinement, and advances the material track by actual arc length. This avoids piecewise-linear angular-velocity kinks in the first implementation.\n\nExecuted independent tests at finite-difference steps \\(0.012, 0.006, 0.003, 0.0015, 0.00075\\) orbital radians gave maximum selected-contact slip discrepancies approximately \\(0.03109, 0.00843, 0.00215, 0.000542, 0.000136\\), respectively. These converge close to the expected \\(O(h^2)\\), rather than only repeating the analytic identity used in the constructor. Full orientation closure residual about \\(1.1\\times10^{-15}\\), and length/cycle return residual about \\(4.6\\times10^{-13}\\).\n\n## Equation-to-curve issue and remedy\n\nThe previous source mapping squeezed both R and Q into narrow hemisphere bands:\n\n```text\nold polar aperture: 0.48 + 0.20 tanh(display_gain * f(lambda))\ncurrent aperture:   0.78 + 0.58 tanh(display_gain * f(lambda))\n```\n\nThese are explicit geometric *representation choices*, not newly derived equation identities. Angles remain between \\(0.20\\) and \\(1.36\\) radians, keeping the chosen half-sphere assignment. The more expressive mapping allows changing source equations to produce visibly different connector and torus-wall traces.\n\nA fourth browser panel now compares **the previous and current actual torus-wall intersection curves at the same orbital parameters**, and displays RMS and maximum world-distance change in model units and tube-radius percentage. The previous trace appears dimly behind the current trace, both in the same torus coordinate system. Nothing is auto-reselected for visual beauty.\n\n**Expected exact duplicates:** distinct underlying equations can define the same sampled scalar representative (e.g. \\(\\cos\\lambda\\) for both an ideal spin-precession expectation and a selected circular-orbit coordinate). If selected in the same input port under identical settings, they should produce the same mapped trace. The comparison panel explicitly calls out zero difference. **The instrument still does not establish physical equivalence** of two theories.\n\n## Output continuity, no curation\n\nThe torus trace is defined by the first forward intersection of the **single elbow ray** with the implicit torus surface. Geometrically valid wall intersections do not imply continuity of the selected-first-hit branch. The application now reports counts of adjacent-step displacements greater than \\(0.20b\\) and the largest step, without smoothing or deleting events. In one default 1,401-point run, 30 adjacent steps exceeded \\(0.11\\) model units and the largest step was about \\(0.347\\). These are *discontinuity candidates*; determining whether they are true root-branch transitions or very rapid continuous motion requires an additional adaptive-step/root-continuation audit.\n\n**Unresolved:** a mathematical derivative mapping \\(Q\\text{ wrt }R\\), complete arbitrary-field invertibility, real-browser visual acceptance, live-site deployment, and global no-slip at \\(b=a\\). The spherical analemma is one explicit model of the user-intended track, not a claim of recovered solar-ephemeris mechanics.\n\n## Implementation\n\n- [Canonical Whirligig application](index.html)\n- [Website integration instructions](SITES_INTEGRATION.md)\n- [Previous equation catalog and revisions](EQUATION_LIBRARY.md)\n- [Older GrAnn functional investigations (historical, not controlling)](../../../tools/whirligig_rq/GRANN_FUNCTIONAL_RECONSTRUCTION_2026-10-18.md)\n\n\n\n## 2026-11-02 CURRENT: equal-area Analemma, equatorial E/W contacts, polar N/S inputs\n\nThis section supersedes the 2026-10-21 material-curve formula above and the earlier 2026-10-17 east/west R/Q placement. The canonical browser file remains [index.html](index.html).\n\n### Confirmed geometry and terminology\n\n- **R** is a closed equation curve around the **north pole**, wholly in the northern hemisphere.\n- **Q** is a closed equation curve around the **south pole**, wholly in the southern hemisphere.\n- The Analemma is a separate closed spherical figure-eight. Its transverse self-crossing is at the **east equatorial pole** E=(1,0,0); its distinct self-tangential kiss is at the antipodal **west equatorial pole** W=(-1,0,0).\n- The northern lobe winds around the north pole; the southern lobe winds around the south pole.\n- One Analemma circuit means the complete two-lobed closed curve. The inner torus circumference is an even multiple of that complete length.\n- Sphere radius equals torus tube minor radius: b=a, so the sphere great-circle circumference equals the tube cross-section circumference.\n\nThe historical source gives the self-crossing and antipodal self-tangency relationship; the E/W versus N/S placement and the equal-area condition above are the user's later explicit geometric refinements.\n\n### Equal-area curve family and solved shape\n\nOn the unit sphere, define\n\n[\n\beta(t)=ksin tcos^2t,qquad phi(t)=2t,\n]\n\n[\nG(t)=\bigl(cos\betacosphi,;cos\betasinphi,;sin\beta\bigr),quad 0le t<2pi.\n]\n\nThe northern lobe is 0<t<pi; the southern lobe is pi<t<2pi. The equal-area interpretation used here is that the **combined two-lobe area** equals the remaining equatorial area. Thus each lobe encloses pi b^2, both lobes enclose 2 pi b^2, and the complement also has area 2 pi b^2.\n\nThe area equation is\n\n[\n2int_0^pi[1-sin(ksin tcos^2t)],dt=pi.\n]\n\nIts first regular root is\n\n[\n\boxed{k=2.63499709629253}.\n]\n\nThe maximum lobe latitude is 58.11000154 degrees. At E, the two branch tangent vectors in local azimuth/latitude components are proportional to (2,k) and (2,-k), so the crossing is transverse. At W, both tangent vectors are proportional to (2,0), while their second-order latitude curvature has opposite sign, giving the intended tangential kiss. The curve is regular; its minimum parameter speed on the unit sphere is greater than 1.\n\n### Length and gearing\n\nThe full material length is\n\n[\nL_A=bint_0^{2pi}sqrt{\beta'(t)^2+4cos^2\beta(t)},dt\n=13.26913503960638,b.\n]\n\nFor the minimum positive even multiple, the inner torus circumference contains two full Analemma circuits:\n\n[\n2pi(R-b)=2L_A,qquad\n\boxed{R/b=5.22369686421446}.\n]\n\nThe browser therefore derives the major radius from the tube/sphere radius. At the retained reference scale b=a=0.55:\n\n| Quantity | Value |\n|---|---:|\n| Sphere and tube radius | 0.55 |\n| Sphere great-circle / tube cross-section circumference | 3.45575191895 |\n| Full physical Analemma length | 7.29802427178 |\n| Torus major radius R | 2.87303327532 |\n| Inner torus circumference | 14.59604854357 |\n| Inner circumference / full Analemma length | 2 exactly, within numerical tolerance |\n\nChanging the scale control changes a=b and derives R proportionally, preserving the equal circumferences and two-circuit gear ratio. The old independent major-radius slider is removed because it allowed the gear constraint to be broken.\n\n### R/Q aperture and W_obble centering\n\nThe R/Q polar aperture adapter is a_RQ=0.78+0.20 tanh(f) radians. R is placed around +z and Q around -z, with opposite azimuths at a common meridional sweep. The aperture gain bounds the normalized crossbar-midpoint offset by sin(0.20)=0.19866933; the default harmonic pair's sampled maximum is about 0.0931 sphere radii. The azimuth/equation mapping remains an explicit representation choice, not a derived field equation.\n\n### Rotational and epistemic limits\n\nThe browser computes the Analemma tangent, normal, and signed geodesic curvature analytically, transports its material point by numerical arc-length inversion, and keeps the existing inner selected-contact no-slip relation. The minimum even winding is now fixed at two full Analemma circuits per torus orbit; the elbow turns remain the LCM of that count and the R/Q sweep count.\n\nEqual area is the chosen geometric balance condition. It has **not** been proven to globally minimize angular acceleration or jerk over all possible spherical figure-eight curves. A separate constrained smoothness optimization would be needed to establish that stronger claim. Equal-radius contact remains nonisolated, so the model still certifies only the nominated contact, not global no-slip across the full contact locus.\n\n### Reproducible calculation\n\nRun python tools/whirligig_rq/validate_equal_area_analemma.py for an independent standard-library calculation of the equal-area root, spherical length, E/W contact types, radius equality, and two-circuit gearing. This is numerical verification of the declared curve family, not proof that the family is uniquely implied by the historical prose.\n"}}

Internal legacy variable names and research filenames may retain `grann` for implementation compatibility, but should not be mistaken for the user's corrected terminology.\n\n## Inner-torus rolling and minimum return\n\nLet the torus major radius be \\(R\\), both sphere radius and torus tube radius be \\(b=a\\), and \\(\\psi\\) parameterize the torus-centerline orbit. The selected contact offset is \\(-b e_r\\).\n\nNo-slip at this nominated inner contact:\n\\[\n\\dot C+\\omega\\times(-b e_r)=0.\n\\]\n\nFor the material Analemma, let \\(s\\) be **actual spherical arc length**, \\(g=G_A(s)\\), \\(t=dg/ds\\), \\(h=g\\times t\\), and \\(\\kappa_g\\) be signed geodesic curvature. The SO(3) lock is\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal Q(\\psi)=[-e_r,\\ e_\\phi,\\ -e_z]\\,[g,t,h]^T,\\qquad\n\\frac{ds}{d\\psi}=\\frac{R}{b}-1.\n\\]\n\nThis produces\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\frac{\\omega}{\\dot\\psi}=\\frac{R}{b}e_z+\n\\left(\\frac{R}{b}-1\\right)\\kappa_g(s)e_r}.\n\\]\n\nThe required \\(+z\\) rolling spin now has the **same sign as orbital travel**, unlike the earlier incorrect outer-wall model. This is *minimal within this declared family and bounded aperture*, not a universal minimum across all possible analemmas.\n\nThe R/Q moving sweep plane still intersects each source curve separately. The one and only perpendicular elbow is phase-locked to \\(\\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)\\), where \\(m\\) is the chosen integer R/Q sweep count per torus orbit. This avoids piecewise-linear angular-velocity kinks in the first implementation.\n\nExecuted independent tests at finite-difference steps \\(0.012, 0.006, 0.003, 0.0015, 0.00075\\) orbital radians gave maximum selected-contact slip discrepancies approximately \\(0.03109, 0.00843, 0.00215, 0.000542, 0.000136\\), respectively. These converge close to the expected \\(O(h^2)\\), rather than only repeating the analytic identity used in the constructor. Full orientation closure residual about \\(1.1\\times10^{-15}\\), and length/cycle return residual about \\(4.6\\times10^{-13}\\).\n\n## Equation-to-curve issue and remedy\n\nThe previous source mapping squeezed both R and Q into narrow hemisphere bands:\n\n```text\nold polar aperture: 0.48 + 0.20 tanh(display_gain * f(lambda))\ncurrent aperture:   0.78 + 0.58 tanh(display_gain * f(lambda))\n```\n\nThese are explicit geometric *representation choices*, not newly derived equation identities. Angles remain between \\(0.20\\) and \\(1.36\\) radians, keeping the chosen half-sphere assignment. The more expressive mapping allows changing source equations to produce visibly different connector and torus-wall traces.\n\nA fourth browser panel now compares **the previous and current actual torus-wall intersection curves at the same orbital parameters**, and displays RMS and maximum world-distance change in model units and tube-radius percentage. The previous trace appears dimly behind the current trace, both in the same torus coordinate system. If selected in the same input port under identical settings, they should produce the same mapped trace. Geometrically valid wall intersections do not imply continuity of the selected-first-hit branch. The application now reports counts of adjacent-step displacements greater than \\(0.20b\\) and the largest step, without smoothing or deleting events. In one default 1,401-point run, 30 adjacent steps exceeded \\(0.11\\) model units and the largest step was about \\(0.347\\). These are *discontinuity candidates*; determining whether they are true root-branch transitions or very rapid continuous motion requires an additional adaptive-step/root-continuation audit.\n\n**Unresolved:** a mathematical derivative mapping \\(Q\\text{ wrt }R\\), complete arbitrary-field invertibility, real-browser visual acceptance, live-site deployment, and global no-slip at \\(b=a\\). The spherical analemma is one explicit model of the user-intended track, not a claim of recovered solar-ephemeris mechanics.\n\n## Implementation\n\n- [Canonical Whirligig application](index.html)\n- [Website integration instructions](SITES_INTEGRATION.md)\n- [Previous equation catalog and revisions](EQUATION_LIBRARY.md)\n- [Older GrAnn functional investigations (historical, not controlling)](../../../tools/whirligig_rq/GRANN_FUNCTIONAL_RECONSTRUCTION_2026-10-18.md)\n\n\n\n## 2026-11-02 CURRENT: equal-area Analemma, equatorial E/W contacts, polar N/S inputs\n\nThis section supersedes the 2026-10-21 material-curve formula above and the earlier 2026-10-17 east/west R/Q placement. The canonical browser file remains [index.html](index.html).\n\n### Confirmed geometry and terminology\n\n- **R** is a closed equation curve around the **north pole**, wholly in the northern hemisphere.\n- **Q** is a closed equation curve around the **south pole**, wholly in the southern hemisphere.\n- The Analemma is a separate closed spherical figure-eight. Its transverse self-crossing is at the **east equatorial pole** \\(E=(1,0,0)\\); its distinct self-tangential kiss is at the antipodal **west equatorial pole** \\(W=(-1,0,0)\\).\n- The northern lobe winds around the north pole; the southern lobe winds around the south pole.\n- One Analemma circuit means the complete two-lobed closed curve. The inner torus circumference is an even multiple of that complete length.\n- Sphere radius equals torus tube minor radius: \\(b=a\\), so the sphere great-circle circumference equals the tube cross-section circumference.\n\nThe historical source gives the self-crossing and antipodal self-tangency relationship; the E/W versus N/S placement and the equal-area condition above are the user's later explicit geometric refinements.\n\n### Equal-area curve family and solved shape\n\nOn the unit sphere, define\n\n\\[\n\\beta(t)=k\\sin t\\cos^2t,\\qquad \\phi(t)=2t,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nG(t)=\\bigl(\\cos\\beta\\cos\\phi,\\;\\cos\\beta\\sin\\phi,\\;\\sin\\beta\\bigr),\n\\quad 0\\le t<2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThe northern lobe is \\(0<t<\\pi\\); the southern lobe is \\(\\pi<t<2\\pi\\). The equal-area interpretation used here is that the **combined two-lobe area** equals the remaining equatorial area. Thus each lobe encloses \\(\\pi b^2\\), both lobes enclose \\(2\\pi b^2\\), and the complement also has area \\(2\\pi b^2\\).\n\nThe area equation is\n\n\\[\n2\\int_0^\\pi\\left[1-\\sin\\left(k\\sin t\\cos^2t\\right)\\right]dt=\\pi.\n\\]\n\nIts first regular root is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{k=2.63499709629253}.\n\\]\n\nThe maximum lobe latitude is \\(58.11000154^\\circ\\). At E, the two branch tangent vectors in local azimuth/latitude components are proportional to \\((2,k)\\) and \\((2,-k)\\), so the crossing is transverse. At W, both tangent vectors are proportional to \\((2,0)\\), while their second-order latitude curvature has opposite sign, giving the intended tangential kiss. The curve is regular; its minimum parameter speed on the unit sphere is greater than 1.\n\n### Length and gearing\n\nThe full material length is\n\n\\[\nL_A=b\\int_0^{2\\pi}\\sqrt{\\beta'(t)^2+4\\cos^2\\beta(t)}\\,dt\n=13.26913503960638\\,b.\n\\]\n\nFor the minimum positive even multiple, the inner torus circumference contains two full Analemma circuits:\n\n\\[\n2\\pi(R-b)=2L_A,\\qquad\n\\boxed{R/b=5.22369686421446}.\n\\]\n\nThe browser therefore derives the major radius from the tube/sphere radius. At the retained reference scale \\(b=a=0.55\\):\n\n| Quantity | Value |\n|---|---:|\n| Sphere and tube radius | 0.55 |\n| Sphere great-circle / tube cross-section circumference | 3.45575191895 |\n| Full physical Analemma length | 7.29802427178 |\n| Torus major radius \\(R\\) | 2.87303327532 |\n| Inner torus circumference | 14.59604854357 |\n| Inner circumference / full Analemma length | 2 exactly, within numerical tolerance |\n\nChanging the scale control changes \\(a=b\\) and derives \\(R\\) proportionally, preserving the equal circumferences and two-circuit gear ratio. The old independent major-radius slider is removed because it allowed the gear constraint to be broken.\n\n### R/Q aperture and W_obble centering\n\nThe R/Q polar aperture adapter is \\(a_{RQ}=0.78+0.20\\tanh(f)\\) radians. R is placed around \\(+z\\) and Q around \\(-z\\), with opposite azimuths at a common meridional sweep. The aperture gain bounds the normalized crossbar-midpoint offset by \\(\\sin(0.20)=0.19866933\\); the default harmonic pair's sampled maximum is about \\(0.0931\\) sphere radii. Across the 84 one-port profile configurations tested, the largest sampled offset is \\(0.12914\\) sphere radii. The azimuth/equation mapping remains an explicit representation choice, not a derived field equation.\n\n### Rotational and epistemic limits\n\nThe browser computes the Analemma tangent, normal, and signed geodesic curvature analytically, transports its material point by numerical arc-length inversion, and keeps the existing inner selected-contact no-slip relation. The minimum even winding is now fixed at two full Analemma circuits per torus orbit; the elbow turns remain the LCM of that count and the R/Q sweep count.\n\nEqual area is the chosen geometric balance condition. It has **not** been proven to globally minimize angular acceleration or jerk over all possible spherical figure-eight curves. A separate constrained smoothness optimization would be needed to establish that stronger claim. Equal-radius contact remains nonisolated, so the model still certifies only the nominated contact, not global no-slip across the full contact locus.\n\n### Reproducible calculation\n\nRun python tools/whirligig_rq/validate_equal_area_analemma.py for an independent standard-library calculation of the equal-area root, spherical length, E/W contact types, radius equality, and two-circuit gearing. ## [1262] ASSISTANT · 2026-11-02T07:23:22.900Z

**The deployment did succeed.** I checked the actual GitHub Actions run, not just the commit status. Its `deploy` job passed all steps, including the Whirligig-only route test, upload, and GitHub Pages deployment.

The branch has advanced since that commit, so I’m checking the current `main` version rather than assuming the deployed snapshot is still the latest source.

I inspected the actual GitHub Pages artifact, then rendered its Whirligig page in Chromium at desktop and mobile sizes. There are some good results, and one important mechanical problem.

**The published route is [Whirligig R/Q](https://satobloc.github.io/HsH/laboratory/whirligig/).** The path is `/laboratory/whirligig/`, not `/instruments/whirligig/`.

The current `main` branch has advanced since deployment, but the four Whirligig files and its build workflow are unchanged from the deployed commit. I made no repository changes during this review.

## What checks out

<badge color="success">Geometry and gearing verified</badge>

| Quantity | Calculated value |
|---|---:|
| Sphere radius = tube radius, \(a=b\) | 0.55 |
| Sphere great-circle circumference | 3.455752 |
| Tube cross-section circumference | 3.455752 |
| Major torus radius, \(R\) | 2.873033 |
| Full Analemma length | 7.298024 |
| Inner torus circumference | 14.596049 |
| Inner circumference / Analemma length | **2.000000** |

The equal-area parameter independently reproduces \(k=2.63499709629\). The major radius is correctly derived from the scale, so changing the tube/sphere radius preserves the gearing.

The browser checks were also encouraging:

- All 42 equation profiles tested in both R and Q positions: **84 configurations**.
- 1,401 orbital samples per configuration.
- No JavaScript exceptions.
- No missing torus intersections.
- Zero north/south hemisphere violations.
- Crossbar perpendicularity and selected-contact slip residuals remain near machine precision.
- SVG export produces a valid file.
- Mobile layout has no horizontal overflow.

## The important problem: Curvy Lisa

<badge color="danger">Not yet mechanically validated</badge>

The output trace is not continuous.

At the default settings, I measured **49 adjacent trace jumps greater than 0.2 tube radii**, with the largest jump approximately **2.735 model units**. The trace closes at the end of the orbit, but that tiny closure residual hides the internal discontinuities.

I dug into the actual ray/torus intersections. The problem is more specific than a general numerical precision issue:

1. The elbow ray intersects the *entire torus surface*. The code does not constrain the hit to the inward-facing half of the tube.
2. Of the 1,401 default samples, only **546** land on the inward-facing radial half. The other **855** land on the outward-facing half.
3. The ray can have multiple positive intersections. When a pair of intersections appears or disappears at a tangency, the current first-hit selection can jump to another intersection.

The code's tiny `Selected INNER wall residual` is checking the sphere's nominated Donomphulon contact. It does **not** demonstrate that the elbow's Curvy Lisa trace stays on the inner wall.

This is the next thing I would fix. We need an explicit inner-wall contact constraint and a continuous intersection-branch rule. Simply increasing the ray solver's sampling resolution or smoothing the plotted trace would conceal the problem rather than solve it.

## Visual review

<grid columns={2} gap={2}>
  <grid-item>
    <AsyncImage query="dark technical 3D scientific torus sphere geometry simulation visualization" aspectRatio="5:4" shop_eligible={false}/>
    <caption>Overall apparatus: readable, though the mechanism occupies a relatively small portion of its panel.</caption>
  </grid-item>
  <grid-item>
    <AsyncImage query="scientific spherical figure eight geometric curves wireframe visualization" aspectRatio="5:4" shop_eligible={false}/>
    <caption>Body-frame geometry: the polar R/Q placement and equatorial Analemma contacts are visible.</caption>
  </grid-item>
</grid>

One small interface defect: the body-frame panel's heading overlaps the canvas's own “Analemma figure-eight material track” annotation. This happens on both desktop and mobile. Moving or removing that canvas annotation would resolve it.

## My assessment

The equal-area Analemma and the two-circuit rotation ratio are sound as a declared geometric construction. The R/Q follower geometry is behaving well. But **the elbow's actual contact with the torus is not yet faithful to the intended inner-wall mechanism**, and that compromises the Curvy Lisa output.

I would leave the Analemma and gear dimensions alone for now. The next pass should concentrate on solving and continuously tracking the elbow's inner-wall intersection, then revisit rotational smoothness. Equal area has not yet been shown to minimize rotational acceleration.

[Canonical source](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/index.html) · [Successful Pages deployment](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/actions/runs/41401033434)

I can take that next pass while keeping the existing gear ratio, sphere/tube equality, and R/Q arrangement fixed.

import math
from scipy.integrate import quad
from scipy.optimize import brentq

def beta(t,k):
    return k*math.sin(t)*math.cos(t)**2

def area_lobe(k):
    return 2*quad(lambda t: 1-math.sin(beta(t,k)), 0, math.pi, epsabs=1e-13, epsrel=1e-13)[0]

k=brentq(lambda k: area_lobe(k)-math.pi, 2.5, 3.0, xtol=1e-14)
L=quad(lambda t: math.hypot(k*math.cos(t)*(1-3*math.sin(t)**2), 2*math.cos(beta(t,k))),0,2*math.pi,epsabs=1e-12,epsrel=1e-12)[0]
ratio=1+2*L/(2*math.pi)
b=.55
R=ratio*b
print({"k":k,"lobe_area":area_lobe(k),"L_over_b":L,"R_over_b":ratio,"b":b,"R":R,"sphere_tube_circ":2*math.pi*b,"analemma_length":L*b,"inner_circ":2*math.pi*(R-b),"inner_over_analemma":2*math.pi*(R-b)/(L*b)})

import numpy as np, math
from scipy.integrate import simpson
K=2.6349970962925298
Lunit=13.269135039606383
q=1+2*Lunit/(2*math.pi)
delta=q-1
N=200001
t=np.linspace(0,2*math.pi,N,endpoint=False)
s=np.sin(t); c=np.cos(t)
beta=K*s*c**2
bp=K*c*(1-3*s**2)
bpp=K*s*(9*s**2-7)
sb=np.sin(beta); cb=np.cos(beta); sp=np.sin(2*t); cp=np.cos(2*t)
g=np.stack([cb*cp,cb*sp,sb],axis=1)
eb=np.stack([-sb*cp,-sb*sp,cb],axis=1)
ep=np.stack([-sp,cp,np.zeros_like(t)],axis=1)
v1=bp[:,None]*eb+2*cb[:,None]*ep
v2=(bpp+4*sb*cb)[:,None]*eb+(-4*bp*sb)[:,None]*ep-(bp**2+4*cb**2)[:,None]*g
speed=np.linalg.norm(v1,axis=1)
kg=np.einsum('ij,ij->i',g,np.cross(v1,v2))/speed**3
dt=2*math.pi/N
kg_t=(np.roll(kg,-1)-np.roll(kg,1))/(2*dt)
kg_s=kg_t/speed
radial_spin=delta*kg
omega_norm=np.sqrt(radial_spin**2+q**2)
alpha_norm=np.sqrt(delta**4*kg_s**2+delta**2*kg**2)
# Average over psi: t loop is traversed twice and dpsi = speed dt / delta
weighted= speed/delta
Jrot=2*simpson(alpha_norm**2*weighted,dx=dt)
rms_alpha=math.sqrt(Jrot/(2*math.pi))
print({
"R_over_b":q,"delta":delta,
"max_abs_kg":float(np.max(np.abs(kg))),
"max_abs_radial_spin":float(np.max(np.abs(radial_spin))),
"omega_norm_min":float(np.min(omega_norm)),
"omega_norm_max":float(np.max(omega_norm)),
"omega_norm_rms":float(math.sqrt((2*simpson(omega_norm**2*weighted,dx=dt))/(2*math.pi))),
"angular_accel_norm_max_per_psi2":float(np.max(alpha_norm)),
"angular_accel_norm_rms_per_psi2":float(rms_alpha),
"Jrot":float(Jrot),
"kg_mean":float(np.mean(kg)),
"kg_rms":float(math.sqrt(np.mean(kg**2)))
})

def smooth_metrics(N):
    t=np.linspace(0,2*math.pi,N,endpoint=False)
    s=np.sin(t); c=np.cos(t)
    be=K*s*c**2
    bp=K*c*(1-3*s**2)
    bpp=K*s*(9*s**2-7)
    sb=np.sin(be); cb=np.cos(be); sp=np.sin(2*t); cp=np.cos(2*t)
    g=np.stack([cb*cp,cb*sp,sb],axis=1)
    eb=np.stack([-sb*cp,-sb*sp,cb],axis=1)
    ep=np.stack([-sp,cp,np.zeros_like(t)],axis=1)
    v1=bp[:,None]*eb+2*cb[:,None]*ep
    v2=(bpp+4*sb*cb)[:,None]*eb+(-4*bp*sb)[:,None]*ep-(bp**2+4*cb**2)[:,None]*g
    speed=np.linalg.norm(v1,axis=1)
    kg=np.einsum('ij,ij->i',g,np.cross(v1,v2))/speed**3
    dt=2*math.pi/N
    kg_t=(np.roll(kg,-1)-np.roll(kg,1))/(2*dt)
    kg_s=kg_t/speed
    alpha=np.sqrt(delta**4*kg_s**2+delta**2*kg**2)
    weight=speed/delta
    J=2*simpson(alpha**2*weight,dx=dt)
    return np.max(np.abs(kg)),np.max(alpha),math.sqrt(J/(2*math.pi)),J
for N in [10001,20001,40001,80001,160001,320001]:
    print(N,smooth_metrics(N))

## [1380] ASSISTANT · 2026-11-02T08:37:24.346Z

Agreed. The clean way to impose that equality is to define **sphere roll as the Analemma's material phase**, measured in the torus-co-rotating frame. Then there is one roll clock, not two competing ones.

The existing gear relation gives

\[
\frac{2\pi(R/b-1)b}{L_A}=2
\]

so the sphere completes exactly two Analemma circuits per torus orbit. Define the common phase as \(\phi_s=2\psi\). The minimum even elbow lock is therefore

\[
\boxed{\phi_e=2\phi_s=4\psi}
\]

That gives **four elbow rotations per torus orbit**. The \(R/b=5.223697\) axial-spin coefficient remains in the inertial-frame rolling equation, but it is not a separate phase clock. 

**The revised rotation law is committed to `main` and verified by repository readback.**

The instrument now has:
- Sphere roll / Analemma: **2 circuits per torus orbit**.
- Elbow: **4 rotations per torus orbit**, exactly 2× sphere roll.
- R/Q sweep: remains independently selectable from 1 to 6 turns, without changing the elbow ratio.
- Minimum shared return: one torus orbit.

I also removed the obsolete LCM calculation and updated the UI readouts and technical documentation.

**Numerical checks**
- Sphere-roll equality residual: \(4.4\times10^{-16}\).
- Elbow ratio residual: \(8.9\times10^{-16}\).
- All six R/Q sweep settings satisfy the one-orbit closure.
- JavaScript syntax and source assertions pass.

**One important remaining mechanical issue:** I reran a 1,401-phase Python reconstruction using exact torus-ray quartic roots. The new elbow law produces 592 inward-facing first hits and 809 outward-facing first hits. The previous law produced 546 inward-facing hits. The worst adjacent trace jump decreased from 2.735 to 2.251 model units, but the number of jumps above \(0.11b\) increased from 49 to 73.

So the new rotation lock is working mathematically, but the elbow still does not reliably trace the *inner* torus wall. I've clarified that distinction in the UI rather than allowing its sphere-contact diagnostic to imply otherwise.

**Files:** [Instrument](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/index.html) · [Derivation](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/ANALEMMA_CORRECTION_2026-10-21.md) · [Numerical validator](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/tools/whirligig_rq/validate_equal_area_analemma.py) · [Latest UI commit](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/commit/37daf1256c0f21a23e3686fd7f3d12d70cf8e286)

I have not verified completion of the GitHub Pages deployment or fetched the live page. The repository changes are confirmed; live publication is not yet confirmed.

The next mechanical problem is now sharply defined: **make the elbow's four-turn motion maintain continuous inward-facing contact**, without disturbing the common roll phase. <MemoryCite />

constraints\u2026</div><button id=\"evenGear\" type=\"button\">Restore minimum 2-circuit gear</button></section>\n<p class=\"foot\">This browser reconstruction preserves the historical <b>a=b</b> limiting setup: the sphere radius equals the torus tube minor radius, so their great-circle and tube cross-section circumferences match. The equal-area Analemma candidate has one lobe around the north pole and one around the south pole; the lobes meet transversely at the east equatorial pole and tangentially at the west equatorial pole. The area-balance parameter is numerically solved, and the full material length sets the minimum even gearing: two complete Analemma circuits per inner-torus circumference. Sphere roll is defined by this same Analemma material phase, so both are two circuits per torus orbit; the elbow rotates at the minimum even multiple, twice that phase (four rotations per orbit). The inertial axial-spin ratio R/b remains a component of the rolling angular velocity, not a second phase clock. The major radius is derived from that ratio; the tube/sphere radius is the overall scale control. The selected contact obeys the analytic no-slip condition at one nominated point only; because equal radii create a nonisolated contact set, this does <b>not</b> certify no-slip across every point of contact. There is no separate pen or projector. The only tracing member is the single gimbal elbow, constrained perpendicular to the moving crossbar. The inner contact is Donomphulon; P_ivot is the separate outer radial point, with BigRad joining the radial construction. The R/Q equation-to-sphere mapping is an explicit representation choice, not a derived physical law. Equal area is a geometric balance condition, not yet a proof of globally minimum angular acceleration. Legacy GrAnn identifiers are implementation history only; the user-facing component is Analemma. This is not a certified physical bearing model and does not establish equation isomorphism. Research reference: <a href=\"https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/tree/main/tools/whirligig_rq\">Whirligig R/Q Python solver</a>.</p></main>\n<script>(()=>{'use strict';const $=s=>document.querySelector(s),PI=Math.PI,TWO=2*PI,ANALEMMA_K=2.6349970962925298,ANALEMMA_UNIT_LENGTH=13.269135039606383,ANALEMMA_CIRCUITS=2,ELBOW_ROLL_MULTIPLE=2,GEAR_RATIO=1+ANALEMMA_CIRCUITS*ANALEMMA_UNIT_LENGTH/TWO,mc=$('#mechanism'),oc=$('#output'),dc=$('#detail'),diffC=$('#difference'),m=mc.getContext('2d'),o=oc.getContext('2d'),dctx=dc.getContext('2d'),diffCtx=diffC.getContext('2d'),inputs=[...document.querySelectorAll('[data-key]')];let run=true,show=true,phase=0,az=.7,el=.45,drag=false,px=0,py=0,last=performance.now(),data=[],cfg=null,previousTrace=null,previousLabel='',currentLabel='';\nconst add=(a,b)=>a.map((x,i)=>x+b[i]),sub=(a,b)=>a.map((x,i)=>x-b[i]),mul=(a,k)=>a.map(x=>x*k),dot=(a,b)=>a.reduce((v,x,i)=>v+x*b[i],0),cross=(a,b)=>[a[1]*b[2]-a[2]*b[1],a[2]*b[0]-a[0]*b[2],a[0]*b[1]-a[1]*b[0]],norm=a=>Math.hypot(...a),unit=a=>mul(a,1/Math.max(1e-12,norm(a)));function Rx(v,t){let c=Math.cos(t),s=Math.sin(t);return[v[0],c*v[1]-s*v[2],s*v[1]+c*v[2]]}function Ry(v,t){let c=Math.cos(t),s=Math.sin(t);return[c*v[0]+s*v[2],v[1],-s*v[0]+c*v[2]]}\nfunction params(){const p=Object.fromEntries(inputs.map(x=>[x.dataset.key,+x.value]));p.major=GEAR_RATIO*p.minor;return p}\nlet N=241,sharedTurns=1,curveR=null,curveQ=null;\nconst EQUATIONS={\n\"harm_r\":{group:\"Demonstration\",title:\"R harmonic source\",formula:\"f(\u03bb) = cos(2\u03bb) + (3/11) sin(3\u03bb)\",kind:\"Synthetic demonstration\",meaning:\"Periodic scalar test input; with display gain 0.55 matches the original R harmonic coefficients.\",limits:\"Demonstration only. {"path":"/GitHub/link_6a1a5af1b40c8191affccbb98ac60fa3/update_file","args":{"repository_full_name":"Satobloc/HsH","path":"PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/ANALEMMA_CORRECTION_2026-10-21.md","content":"# Whirligig / Analemma: terminology and functional reconstruction\n\n**Date:** 2026-10-21. **Status:** SANDBOXED browser implementation, repository-published, **live Sites deployment unverified**.\n\n## Direct user correction and provenance\n\nThe early records' **GrAnn / Great Annulum** was a mistaken term. The user intended an **Analemma**. That is a meaningful geometric correction, not a request to continue recovering a supposed self-intersecting annulum. Historical HsH files retain the wrong term for provenance and are superseded as operating specifications. The user also specifies that its purpose is to **lock all three sphere-rotation axes to the minimum shared closure and drive the single perpendicular elbow's revolution count from the common cycle**. The sphere is to roll on the **inner radial torus surface**.\n\nFor astronomical context only, the conventional solar analemma is the figure-eight locus of apparent solar declination versus equation of time at a fixed mean time of day. See the US Naval Observatory's [Equation of Time](https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/eqtime) explanation. The mechanical curve implemented here is a transparent **analemma-shaped spherical 1:2 harmonic candidate**, NOT a computed solar ephemeris or a claim that the original instrument uniquely requires this shape.\n\n## Implemented 3D material contact curve\n\nLet \\(t\\in[0,2\\pi]\\) run over one material Analemma circuit and \\(A>0\\) control its spherical aperture:\n\n\\[\nG_A(t)=\\frac{(-1,\\ A\\sin t,\\ A(\\sin2t+0.27\\sin t))}{\\|(-1,\\ A\\sin t,\\ A(\\sin2t+0.27\\sin t))\\|}.\n\\]\n\nThis is a closed self-intersecting curve on the **unit sphere** with unequal lobes. \\(G_A(0)=G_A(\\pi)=(-1,0,0)\\), but the two branches have distinct tangent directions. Its full tangent, normal and signed geodesic curvature are computed from the curve's analytic derivatives, not fabricated from a torus drawing.\n\nThe older reconstruction's circular carrier has been replaced in both world and sphere-body displays. The UI labels it **Analemma**. Internal legacy variable names and research filenames may retain `grann` for implementation compatibility, but should not be mistaken for the user's corrected terminology.\n\n## Inner-torus rolling and minimum return\n\nLet the torus major radius be \\(R\\), both sphere radius and torus tube radius be \\(b=a\\), and \\(\\psi\\) parameterize the torus-centerline orbit. Define unit radial \\(e_r\\), orbital tangent \\(e_\\phi\\), vertical \\(e_z\\).\n\nThe selected point on the **inner** torus wall is \\(Donomphulon=(R-b)e_r\\). The separately named **outer** radial point remains \\(P_{ivot}=(R+b)e_r\\). Sphere center \\(C=Re_r\\). The selected contact offset is \\(-b e_r\\).\n\nNo-slip at this nominated inner contact:\n\\[\n\\dot C+\\omega\\times(-b e_r)=0.\n\\]\n\nFor the material Analemma, let \\(s\\) be **actual spherical arc length**, \\(g=G_A(s)\\), \\(t=dg/ds\\), \\(h=g\\times t\\), and \\(\\kappa_g\\) be signed geodesic curvature. The SO(3) lock is\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal Q(\\psi)=[-e_r,\\ e_\\phi,\\ -e_z]\\,[g,t,h]^T,\\qquad\n\\frac{ds}{d\\psi}=\\frac{R}{b}-1.\n\\]\n\nThis produces\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\frac{\\omega}{\\dot\\psi}=\\frac{R}{b}e_z+\n\\left(\\frac{R}{b}-1\\right)\\kappa_g(s)e_r}.\n\\]\n\nThe required \\(+z\\) rolling spin now has the **same sign as orbital travel**, unlike the earlier incorrect outer-wall model. The radial spin component rotates through **x and y** as the sphere goes around the torus, so all three spatial axes participate. This is mathematically an **inner selected-contact** constraint, not global no-slip over the nonisolated \\(b=a\\) contact locus.\n\nLet \\(L_G(A)\\) be the true spherical arclength of one material Analemma. One torus orbit moves through \\(2\\pi(R/b-1)\\) of material arc length. The model searches for the **smallest positive even** winding count \\(n\\), subject to its openly stated admissible aperture \\(0<A\\le2\\), satisfying\n\n\\[\nn L_G(A)=2\\pi\\left(\\frac{R}{b}-1\\right).\n\\]\n\nWith \\(R=1.65\\), \\(b=0.55\\), the minimum is \\(n=2\\), numerical \\(A\\approx0.935206924\\), and \\(L_G\\approx2\\pi\\). This is *minimal within this declared family and bounded aperture*, not a universal minimum across all possible analemmas.\n\nThe R/Q moving sweep plane still intersects each source curve separately. The one and only perpendicular elbow is phase-locked to \\(\\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)\\), where \\(m\\) is the chosen integer R/Q sweep count per torus orbit. No extra projector and no independent elbow-turn slider.\n\n### Numerical transport detail\n\nThe current browser integrates Analemma arclength with composite Simpson quadrature, inverts its monotone \\(s(t)\\) table with a bracket and a local Newton/Simpson refinement, and advances the material track by actual arc length. This avoids piecewise-linear angular-velocity kinks in the first implementation.\n\nExecuted independent tests at finite-difference steps \\(0.012, 0.006, 0.003, 0.0015, 0.00075\\) orbital radians gave maximum selected-contact slip discrepancies approximately \\(0.03109, 0.00843, 0.00215, 0.000542, 0.000136\\), respectively. These converge close to the expected \\(O(h^2)\\), rather than only repeating the analytic identity used in the constructor. Full orientation closure residual about \\(1.1\\times10^{-15}\\), and length/cycle return residual about \\(4.6\\times10^{-13}\\).\n\n## Equation-to-curve issue and remedy\n\nThe previous source mapping squeezed both R and Q into narrow hemisphere bands:\n\n```text\nold polar aperture: 0.48 + 0.20 tanh(display_gain * f(lambda))\ncurrent aperture:   0.78 + 0.58 tanh(display_gain * f(lambda))\n```\n\nThese are explicit geometric *representation choices*, not newly derived equation identities. Angles remain between \\(0.20\\) and \\(1.36\\) radians, keeping the chosen half-sphere assignment. The more expressive mapping allows changing source equations to produce visibly different connector and torus-wall traces.\n\nA fourth browser panel now compares **the previous and current actual torus-wall intersection curves at the same orbital parameters**, and displays RMS and maximum world-distance change in model units and tube-radius percentage. The previous trace appears dimly behind the current trace, both in the same torus coordinate system. Nothing is auto-reselected for visual beauty.\n\n**Expected exact duplicates:** distinct underlying equations can define the same sampled scalar representative (e.g. \\(\\cos\\lambda\\) for both an ideal spin-precession expectation and a selected circular-orbit coordinate). If selected in the same input port under identical settings, they should produce the same mapped trace. The comparison panel explicitly calls out zero difference. **The instrument still does not establish physical equivalence** of two theories.\n\n## Output continuity, no curation\n\nThe torus trace is defined by the first forward intersection of the **single elbow ray** with the implicit torus surface. Geometrically valid wall intersections do not imply continuity of the selected-first-hit branch. The application now reports counts of adjacent-step displacements greater than \\(0.20b\\) and the largest step, without smoothing or deleting events. In one default 1,401-point run, 30 adjacent steps exceeded \\(0.11\\) model units and the largest step was about \\(0.347\\). These are *discontinuity candidates*; determining whether they are true root-branch transitions or very rapid continuous motion requires an additional adaptive-step/root-continuation audit.\n\n**Unresolved:** a mathematical derivative mapping \\(Q\\text{ wrt }R\\), complete arbitrary-field invertibility, real-browser visual acceptance, live-site deployment, and global no-slip at \\(b=a\\). The spherical analemma is one explicit model of the user-intended track, not a claim of recovered solar-ephemeris mechanics.\n\n## Implementation\n\n- [Canonical Whirligig application](index.html)\n- [Website integration instructions](SITES_INTEGRATION.md)\n- [Previous equation catalog and revisions](EQUATION_LIBRARY.md)\n- [Older GrAnn functional investigations (historical, not controlling)](../../../tools/whirligig_rq/GRANN_FUNCTIONAL_RECONSTRUCTION_2026-10-18.md)\n\n\n\n## 2026-11-02 CURRENT: equal-area Analemma, equatorial E/W contacts, polar N/S inputs\n\nThis section supersedes the 2026-10-21 material-curve formula above and the earlier 2026-10-17 east/west R/Q placement. The canonical browser file remains [index.html](index.html).\n\n### Confirmed geometry and terminology\n\n- **R** is a closed equation curve around the **north pole**, wholly in the northern hemisphere.\n- **Q** is a closed equation curve around the **south pole**, wholly in the southern hemisphere.\n- The Analemma is a separate closed spherical figure-eight. Its transverse self-crossing is at the **east equatorial pole** \\(E=(1,0,0)\\); its distinct self-tangential kiss is at the antipodal **west equatorial pole** \\(W=(-1,0,0)\\).\n- The northern lobe winds around the north pole; the southern lobe winds around the south pole.\n- One Analemma circuit means the complete two-lobed closed curve. The inner torus circumference is an even multiple of that complete length.\n- Sphere radius equals torus tube minor radius: \\(b=a\\), so the sphere great-circle circumference equals the tube cross-section circumference.\n\nThe historical source gives the self-crossing and antipodal self-tangency relationship; the E/W versus N/S placement and the equal-area condition above are the user's later explicit geometric refinements.\n\n### Equal-area curve family and solved shape\n\nOn the unit sphere, define\n\n\\[\n\\beta(t)=k\\sin t\\cos^2t,\\qquad \\phi(t)=2t,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nG(t)=\\bigl(\\cos\\beta\\cos\\phi,\\;\\cos\\beta\\sin\\phi,\\;\\sin\\beta\\bigr),\n\\quad 0\\le t<2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThe northern lobe is \\(0<t<\\pi\\); the southern lobe is \\(\\pi<t<2\\pi\\). The equal-area interpretation used here is that the **combined two-lobe area** equals the remaining equatorial area. Thus each lobe encloses \\(\\pi b^2\\), both lobes enclose \\(2\\pi b^2\\), and the complement also has area \\(2\\pi b^2\\).\n\nThe area equation is\n\n\\[\n2\\int_0^\\pi\\left[1-\\sin\\left(k\\sin t\\cos^2t\\right)\\right]dt=\\pi.\n\\]\n\nIts first regular root is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{k=2.63499709629253}.\n\\]\n\nThe maximum lobe latitude is \\(58.11000154^\\circ\\). At E, the two branch tangent vectors in local azimuth/latitude components are proportional to \\((2,k)\\) and \\((2,-k)\\), so the crossing is transverse. At W, both tangent vectors are proportional to \\((2,0)\\), while their second-order latitude curvature has opposite sign, giving the intended tangential kiss. The curve is regular; its minimum parameter speed on the unit sphere is greater than 1.\n\n### Length and gearing\n\nThe full material length is\n\n\\[\nL_A=b\\int_0^{2\\pi}\\sqrt{\\beta'(t)^2+4\\cos^2\\beta(t)}\\,dt\n=13.26913503960638\\,b.\n\\]\n\nFor the minimum positive even multiple, the inner torus circumference contains two full Analemma circuits:\n\n\\[\n2\\pi(R-b)=2L_A,\\qquad\n\\boxed{R/b=5.22369686421446}.\n\\]\n\nThe browser therefore derives the major radius from the tube/sphere radius. At the retained reference scale \\(b=a=0.55\\):\n\n| Quantity | Value |\n|---|---:|\n| Sphere and tube radius | 0.55 |\n| Sphere great-circle / tube cross-section circumference | 3.45575191895 |\n| Full physical Analemma length | 7.29802427178 |\n| Torus major radius \\(R\\) | 2.87303327532 |\n| Inner torus circumference | 14.59604854357 |\n| Inner circumference / full Analemma length | 2 exactly, within numerical tolerance |\n\nChanging the scale control changes \\(a=b\\) and derives \\(R\\) proportionally, preserving the equal circumferences and two-circuit gear ratio. The old independent major-radius slider is removed because it allowed the gear constraint to be broken.\n\n### R/Q aperture and W_obble centering\n\nThe R/Q polar aperture adapter is \\(a_{RQ}=0.78+0.20\\tanh(f)\\) radians. R is placed around \\(+z\\) and Q around \\(-z\\), with opposite azimuths at a common meridional sweep. The aperture gain bounds the normalized crossbar-midpoint offset by \\(\\sin(0.20)=0.19866933\\); the default harmonic pair's sampled maximum is about \\(0.0931\\) sphere radii. Across the 84 one-port profile configurations tested, the largest sampled offset is \\(0.12914\\) sphere radii. The azimuth/equation mapping remains an explicit representation choice, not a derived field equation.\n\n### Rotational and epistemic limits\n\nThe browser computes the Analemma tangent, normal, and signed geodesic curvature analytically, transports its material point by numerical arc-length inversion, and keeps the existing inner selected-contact no-slip relation. The minimum even winding is now fixed at two full Analemma circuits per torus orbit; the elbow turns remain the LCM of that count and the R/Q sweep count.\n\nEqual area is the chosen geometric balance condition. It has **not** been proven to globally minimize angular acceleration or jerk over all possible spherical figure-eight curves. A separate constrained smoothness optimization would be needed to establish that stronger claim. Equal-radius contact remains nonisolated, so the model still certifies only the nominated contact, not global no-slip across the full contact locus.\n\n### Reproducible calculation\n\nRun python tools/whirligig_rq/validate_equal_area_analemma.py for an independent standard-library calculation of the equal-area root, spherical length, E/W contact types, radius equality, and two-circuit gearing. This is numerical verification of the declared curve family, not proof that the family is uniquely implied by the historical prose.\n\n\n## 2026-11-02 CURRENT: common sphere-roll / Analemma phase and 2\u00d7 elbow lock\n\nThis section supersedes the earlier browser rule that set elbow turns to the LCM of Analemma circuits and R/Q sweep laps. The sphere-roll phase and Analemma material phase are now **one and the same phase**, measured in the torus-co-rotating material frame. The elbow is driven by the minimum positive even multiple of that common phase.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\delta=R/b-1,\\qquad \\ell_A=L_A/b,\n\\]\n\nand let \\(\\psi\\) be the torus orbital angle. The Analemma material arclength advance is\n\n\\[\ns/b=\\delta\\psi.\n\\]\n\nDefine the common sphere-roll / Analemma phase by\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\phi_s=2\\pi\\frac{s}{L_A}\n=2\\pi\\frac{\\delta}{\\ell_A}\\psi}.\n\\]\n\nThe gear condition already imposed by the equal-area Analemma is\n\n\\[\n2\\pi\\delta=2\\ell_A.\n\\]\n\nTherefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\phi_s=2\\psi},\n\\]\n\nwhich is exactly two full sphere-roll / Analemma circuits per torus orbit. The two former descriptions are no longer separate clocks.\n\nThe elbow phase is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\phi_e=2\\phi_s=4\\psi}.\n\\]\n\nThus the minimum even multiplier is 2, and the elbow makes **four rotations per torus orbit**. The R/Q sweep remains an integer number of turns per torus orbit; it no longer changes the elbow gear count. With the current integer sweep control, all phases return after one torus orbit.\n\n**Reference-frame distinction:** the inner-wall no-slip equation still gives the inertial-frame axial angular-velocity component\n\n\\[\n\\omega_z/\\dot\\psi=R/b=5.2236968642.\n\\]\n\nThat is a component of the full three-axis angular velocity in the laboratory frame. It is not a second material-phase clock and is not to be forced numerically equal to the two Analemma circuits. The common roll phase is the sphere's Analemma material phase in the co-rotating frame. Replacing the no-slip axial component by 2 would break the existing inner-contact rolling equation and the derived equal-area gear relation.\n\nThis change modifies the elbow's rotation law only. It does not, by itself, resolve the separately documented first-hit branch discontinuities or guarantee that the elbow ray intersects the inward-facing half of the torus at every phase.\n","sha":"da6632f4d2ac56de90932ffba158f4bd4375d85a","message":"Lock Whirligig elbow to twice the common sphere-roll phase","branch":"main"}}

This code does too.\n\n## Run\n\n```bash\npython -m pip install -r requirements.txt\npython whirligig.py --input example_equations.json --out output --search\npython plot_mechanics.py --input example_equations.json --out mechanics_snapshot.png --gif rolling_whirligig.gif\npython validate_mapping.py --input example_equations.json --out mapping_validation.json\npython -m pytest -q\n```\n\n`--input` is optional: a two-harmonic-pair demonstration is built in.\n\n## Input equation adapters\n\nTwo independent specs are supplied as `R` and `Q` in a JSON file. ## [1412] ASSISTANT · 2026-11-02T08:45:07.295Z

import math
from scipy.integrate import quad
from scipy.optimize import brentq

TAU=2*math.pi
def beta(t,k): return k*math.sin(t)*math.cos(t)**2
def beta_p(t,k): return k*math.cos(t)*(1-3*math.sin(t)**2)
def speed(t,k): return math.hypot(beta_p(t,k), 2*math.cos(beta(t,k)))
def lobe_area(k):
    return 2*quad(lambda t: 1-math.sin(beta(t,k)),0,math.pi,epsabs=1e-13)[0]
k=brentq(lambda x:lobe_area(x)-math.pi,2.5,3.0,xtol=1e-14)
L=quad(lambda t:speed(t,k),0,TAU,epsabs=1e-12)[0]
circuits=2
ratio=1+circuits*L/TAU
delta=ratio-1
sphere_roll_turns=TAU*delta/L
elbow_multiple=2
elbow_turns=elbow_multiple*sphere_roll_turns
psi=TAU
sphere_roll_phase=sphere_roll_turns*psi
elbow_phase=elbow_multiple*sphere_roll_phase
{
    "k": k,
    "Analemma_length_over_b": L,
    "R_over_b": ratio,
    "delta": delta,
    "sphere_roll_turns_per_orbit": sphere_roll_turns,
    "sphere_roll_phase_per_orbit_rad": sphere_roll_phase,
    "elbow_multiplier": elbow_multiple,
    "elbow_turns_per_orbit": elbow_turns,
    "elbow_phase_per_orbit_rad": elbow_phase,
    "phase_identity_error": sphere_roll_turns-circuits,
    "elbow_lock_error": elbow_turns-elbow_multiple*circuits
}

    sphere_phase_per_orbit = TAU * delta / ell_A
    elbow_phase_per_orbit = 2 * sphere_phase_per_orbit
    # Normalized turns per complete torus orbit.

    assert abs(elbow_phase_per_orbit - 4) < 1e-12
    assert sweep_laps == round(sweep_laps)

## [1438] ASSISTANT · 2026-11-02T08:46:59.960Z

import numpy as np, math
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.integrate import cumulative_trapezoid

TAU=2*math.pi
b=.55
LA=13.269135039606383
delta=4.22369686421446
R=(1+delta)*b
K=2.6349970962925298

def beta(t): return K*np.sin(t)*np.cos(t)**2
def beta_p(t): return K*np.cos(t)*(1-3*np.sin(t)**2)
def beta_pp(t): return K*np.sin(t)*(9*np.sin(t)**2-7)
def an_frame(t):
    be=beta(t); bp=beta_p(t); bpp=beta_pp(t); p=2*t
    sb,cb,sp,cp=np.sin(be),np.cos(be),np.sin(p),np.cos(p)
    g=np.array([cb*cp,cb*sp,sb])
    eb=np.array([-sb*cp,-sb*sp,cb])
    ep=np.array([-sp,cp,0.])
    v1=eb*bp+ep*(2*cb)
    v2=eb*(bpp+4*sb*cb)+ep*(-4*bp*sb)+g*(-(bp*bp+4*cb*cb))
    speed=np.linalg.norm(v1)
    tangent=v1/speed
    h=np.cross(g,tangent)
    kg=np.dot(g,np.cross(v1,v2))/speed**3
    return g,tangent,h,kg

# Arc-length lookup for material Analemma phase.
nt=200001
ts=np.linspace(0,TAU,nt)
speeds=np.hypot(beta_p(ts),2*np.cos(beta(ts)))
arc=np.concatenate([[0],cumulative_trapezoid(speeds,ts)])
# Correct tiny cumulative-trapezoid error with analytic reference scale.
arc *= LA/arc[-1]

def an_at(psi):
    s=(delta*psi)%LA
    if s<1e-10 or s>LA-1e-10: s=0.
    t=np.interp(s,arc,ts)
    return an_frame(t)

def eq(t,side):
    if side=="r": return .55*(np.cos(2*t)+(3/11)*np.sin(3*t))
    return .60*(np.sin(3*t)+(1/6)*np.cos(5*t))
def bearing(t,side):
    kk=0 if side=="r" else .7
    return t+.11*(np.sin(2*t+kk)-np.sin(kk))+.03*(np.tanh(eq(t,side))-np.tanh(eq(0,side)))
def polar(t,side):
    north=side=="r"
    ap=.78+.20*np.tanh(eq(t,side))
    ph=bearing(t,side)+(0 if north else math.pi)
    return np.array([np.sin(ap)*np.cos(ph),np.sin(ap)*np.sin(ph),(1 if north else -1)*np.cos(ap)])
def follow(alpha,side):
    alpha=alpha%TAU
    t=brentq(lambda t:bearing(t,side)-alpha,0,TAU,xtol=1e-13)
    return polar(t,side)
def qmap(v,g,t,h,er,et,ez):
    return -er*np.dot(g,v)+et*np.dot(t,v)-ez*np.dot(h,v)
def poly_roots_ray(o,d):
    X=np.array([o[0]**2+o[1]**2,2*(o[0]*d[0]+o[1]*d[1]),d[0]**2+d[1]**2])
    Z=np.array([o[2]**2,2*o[2]*d[2],d[2]**2])
    A=np.polynomial.polynomial.polyadd(np.polynomial.polynomial.polyadd(X,Z),[R*R-b*b])
    P=np.polynomial.polynomial.polysub(np.polynomial.polynomial.polymul(A,A),4*R*R*X)
    roots=np.polynomial.polynomial.polyroots(P)
    roots=[float(x.real) for x in roots if abs(x.imag)<1e-7 and x.real>1e-8]
    roots.sort()
    return roots
def sample_hit(psi, elbow_mult=2):
    er=np.array([np.cos(psi),np.sin(psi),0.])
    et=np.array([-np.sin(psi),np.cos(psi),0.])
    ez=np.array([0.,0.,1.])
    g,t,h,kg=an_at(psi)
    Q=lambda v:qmap(v,g,t,h,er,et,ez)
    center=R*er
    sweep=psi
    A=follow(sweep,"r")
    B=follow(sweep,"q")
    pr=center+b*Q(A)
    pq=center+b*Q(B)
    dr=pq-pr
    direction=dr/np.linalg.norm(dr)
    ref=Q(ez)
    if abs(np.dot(ref,direction))>.9: ref=Q(np.array([0.,1.,0.]))
    u=ref-direction*np.dot(ref,direction)
    u=u/np.linalg.norm(u)
    v=np.cross(direction,u); v=v/np.linalg.norm(v)
    roll_phase=2*psi # derived common phase
    theta=elbow_mult*roll_phase
    elbow=u*np.cos(theta)+v*np.sin(theta)
    mid=(pr+pq)/2
    roots=poly_roots_ray(mid,elbow)
    if not roots: return None, roots
    lam=roots[0]
    hit=mid+lam*elbow
    inner=np.hypot(hit[0],hit[1])<R
    return (hit,inner,lam),roots

N=1401
res=[sample_hit(TAU*i/(N-1),2) for i in range(N)]
valid=[x[0] for x in res if x[0] is not None]
inner_count=sum(1 for x in valid if x[1])
jumps=[np.linalg.norm(valid[i][0]-valid[i-1][0]) for i in range(1,len(valid))]
len(valid),inner_count,len(valid)-inner_count,max(jumps),sum(j>.11 for j in jumps),np.percentile(jumps,[50,90,99])

id=\"vmajor\"></output> (derived from Analemma gear)</label>\n<label>Tube & sphere radius a=b <output id=\"va\"></output><input data-key=\"minor\" type=\"range\" min=\".3\" max=\".8\" step=\".05\" speed <output id=\"vspeed\">1.5\u00d7</output><input id=\"speed\" type=\"range\" min=\".25\" max=\"4\" step=\".25\" value=\"1.5\"></label>\n</div><div id=\"stats\" class=\"stats\" role=\"status\">Computing geometry\u2026</div><section class=\"grann-panel\"><strong>Analemma / inner-torus rotational lock</strong><div id=\"grannStatus\" role=\"status\">Computing Analemma constraints\u2026</div><button id=\"evenGear\" type=\"button\">Restore minimum 2-circuit gear</button></section>\n<p class=\"foot\">This browser reconstruction preserves the historical <b>a=b</b> limiting setup: the sphere radius equals the torus tube minor radius, so their great-circle and tube cross-section circumferences match. The equal-area Analemma candidate has one lobe around the north pole and one around the south pole; the lobes meet transversely at the east equatorial pole and tangentially at the west equatorial pole. The area-balance parameter is numerically solved, and the full material length sets the minimum even gearing: two complete Analemma circuits per inner-torus circumference. Sphere roll is defined by this same Analemma material phase, so both are two circuits per torus orbit; the elbow rotates at the minimum even multiple, twice that phase (four rotations per orbit). The inertial axial-spin ratio R/b remains a component of the rolling angular velocity, not a second phase clock. The major radius is derived from that ratio; the tube/sphere radius is the overall scale control. The selected contact obeys the analytic no-slip condition at one nominated point only; because equal radii create a nonisolated contact set, this does <b>not</b> certify no-slip across every point of contact. There is no separate pen or projector. The only tracing member is the single gimbal elbow, constrained perpendicular to the moving crossbar. The inner sphere contact is Donomphulon; P_ivot is the separate outer radial point, with BigRad joining the radial construction. The elbow ray's current first-hit solver intersects the full torus, not only its inward-facing half; wall-hit counts do not certify inner-half elbow contact. The R/Q equation-to-sphere mapping is an explicit representation choice, not a derived physical law. Equal area is a geometric balance condition, not yet a proof of globally minimum angular acceleration. Legacy GrAnn identifiers are implementation history only; the user-facing component is Analemma. This is not a certified physical bearing model and does not establish equation isomorphism. Research reference: <a href=\"https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/tree/main/tools/whirligig_rq\">Whirligig R/Q Python solver</a>.</p></main>\n<script>(()=>{'use strict';const $=s=>document.querySelector(s),PI=Math.PI,TWO=2*PI,ANALEMMA_K=2.6349970962925298,ANALEMMA_UNIT_LENGTH=13.269135039606383,ANALEMMA_CIRCUITS=2,ELBOW_ROLL_MULTIPLE=2,GEAR_RATIO=1+ANALEMMA_CIRCUITS*ANALEMMA_UNIT_LENGTH/TWO,mc=$('#mechanism'),oc=$('#output'),dc=$('#detail'),diffC=$('#difference'),m=mc.getContext('2d'),o=oc.getContext('2d'),dctx=dc.getContext('2d'),diffCtx=diffC.getContext('2d'),inputs=[...document.querySelectorAll('[data-key]')];let run=true,show=true,phase=0,az=.7,el=.45,drag=false,px=0,py=0,last=performance.now(),data=[],cfg=null,previousTrace=null,previousLabel='',currentLabel='';\nconst add=(a,b)=>a.map((x,i)=>x+b[i]),sub=(a,b)=>a.map((x,i)=>x-b[i]),mul=(a,k)=>a.map(x=>x*k),dot=(a,b)=>a.reduce((v,x,i)=>v+x*b[i],0),cross=(a,b)=>[a[1]*b[2]-a[2]*b[1],a[2]*b[0]-a[0]*b[2],a[0]*b[1]-a[1]*b[0]],norm=a=>Math.hypot(...a),unit=a=>mul(a,1/Math.max(1e-12,norm(a)));function Rx(v,t){let c=Math.cos(t),s=Math.sin(t);return[v[0],c*v[1]-s*v[2],s*v[1]+c*v[2]]}function Ry(v,t){let c=Math.cos(t),s=Math.sin(t);return[c*v[0]+s*v[2],v[1],-s*v[0]+c*v[2]]}\nfunction params(){const p=Object.fromEntries(inputs.map(x=>[x.dataset.key,+x.value]));p.major=GEAR_RATIO*p.minor;return p}\nlet N=241,sharedTurns=1,curveR=null,curveQ=null;\nconst EQUATIONS={\n\"harm_r\":{group:\"Demonstration\",title:\"R harmonic source\",formula:\"f(\u03bb) = cos(2\u03bb) + (3/11) sin(3\u03bb)\",kind:\"Synthetic demonstration\",meaning:\"Periodic scalar test input; with display gain 0.55 matches the original R harmonic coefficients.\",limits:\"Demonstration only. ## [1452] ASSISTANT · 2026-11-02T10:17:00.777Z

I meant **the side closest to the donut hole**: the inward-facing radial surface of the torus tube.

Those are two different geometric descriptions:

1. **Sphere-contacting surface:** the particular patch of torus tube that physically touches the sphere.
2. **Donut-hole-facing surface:** the inward radial flank of the tube, facing the central opening.

In the code, I used \(\rho<R\) to identify the second one. I did **not** establish that this is necessarily the same patch as the sphere-contacting surface.

More importantly, the original specification identifies Donomphulon as the inner radial contact, but I should not silently equate that with an independently imposed elbow-tip constraint.

So the distinction matters: **is the elbow supposed to trace the donut-hole-facing flank, or is it supposed to trace the actual sphere-contacting surface?**

## [1457] ASSISTANT · 2026-11-02T10:18:48.979Z

Understood. I introduced a constraint that isn't in the specification. It shouldn't have been there.

The elbow projects wherever its gimbal-directed ray intersects the torus. **No requirement that the hit be on the donut-hole-facing flank, the sphere-contacting surface, or any particular radial half of the torus.**

That changes how we evaluate the instrument:

- Any genuine torus intersection is a valid projection.
- Outward-facing hits are not failures.
- We should not filter intersections by \(\rho<R\).
- The solver should report the actual projected point and handle multiple intersections and tangencies correctly.

The original geometry gets to determine where Curvy Lisa goes. We shouldn't quietly redesign it by imposing a destination.

## [1462] ASSISTANT · 2026-11-02T10:19:56.388Z

I think I can reconstruct the mistake. It was a chain of three conflations, each of which seemed reasonable in isolation but led to an unjustified conclusion.

**1. I conflated two different geometric relationships.**

The original construction names Donomphulon as a point on the inner torus circumference, associated with the sphere's nominated contact geometry. I carried that terminology over to the elbow, which is a separate moving component.

I implicitly assumed that because one part of the mechanism has an inner contact, the elbow must also contact that same side of the torus. That does not follow.

**2. I turned a descriptive phrase into a mathematical constraint.**

The implementation and notes used language such as *inner wall*. I translated that into the condition

\[
\rho < R
\]

where \(R\) is the torus major radius. That identifies the hole-facing radial flank. But it was my operational interpretation, not a requirement established by the specification.

**3. I confused a numerical problem with a mechanical requirement.**

The ray can intersect the torus more than once. Tangencies can appear or disappear, and a naïve first-root solver can jump between intersection branches. I wanted to eliminate those discontinuities by restricting the solver to one side.

That was the fundamental category error: I tried to solve a numerical continuity problem by imposing a physical constraint that the design never specified.

The distinction matters:

- **Geometry:** determines where the elbow projects.
- **Intersection mathematics:** determines how we calculate that projection, including multiple roots and tangencies.
- **Mechanical specification:** determines what the elbow is required to do.

I let the second dictate the third.

The correct approach is to preserve the specified mechanism, calculate its actual projection, and investigate any discontinuities as properties of that geometry. If the resulting trace has surprising behavior, that's something to understand, not something to prohibit in advance.

In short, I mistook a convenient assumption for a design necessity. That was my error. <MemoryCite />

## [1463] USER · 2026-11-02T10:45:55.076Z

The inner wall is intended to be the inside surface of the tube. But... your thinking is somewhat in line with something I've been thinking as well. There are multiple ways to accomplish the result we need, which is: 1) Polar curves capture the entirety of information defined by the input equations; that is, for either curve, its exact input equation can be reproduced directly from the curve. 2) The composite curve captures the totality of the information of both curves simultaneously. 3) The composite curve drawn on the inner surface of the torus should ideally be reverse-engineerable to produce an equation of the composite curve; ideally, a precise one, fully specifying the entirety of the curve (though approximately is acceptable, within some reasonable boundaries). 

So... what I've been thinking, to make the curve more well-behaved, and to force it to reconnect with itself after a finite (or even set) number of rotations, is something like this--
Construct a second crossbar that behaves exactly as the first, except 1) Its contact points with the curves are mirror-flipped... if the first crossbar intersects the northern curve in the eastern hemisphere, then the second intersects it in the western. 2) It swings about its trace of the two curves in the opposite direction, and it rotates in the opposite direction. 3) The elbow of the second crossbar (it's own elbow; neither mechanism is attached to the other anywhere). 4) Instead of tracing a composite curve, the pointer arm is anchored on the inside rim of the donut hole (and by virtue of that, it also intersects the center of the torus and the outer large circumference, 'slicing' the torus bagelwise). 

Constructed this way, I think what we'd have is the sphere rolling and wobbling such that it a) amplifies the wobble of the first crossbar, and b) keeps the projector arm pointed approximately on the outside (in the sense that you meant with the inside surface) of the torus. It would also (I think) force the curve to eventually reconnect with itself.

## [1467] ASSISTANT · 2026-11-02T10:49:38.435Z

I think there's a potentially important idea here. You're describing something more interesting than adding a second projector: **a conjugate mechanism that may turn the first mechanism's wobble into a useful, measurable relative motion, while providing a second geometric reference for reconstructing the trace.**

And I need to correct one thing from my last response: the intended target is still the tube's actual inside surface. What was unjustified was treating \(\rho<R\), the donut-hole-facing radial half, as an adequate definition of that surface. Those are not interchangeable descriptions without a proper geometric derivation.

## 1. The two mechanisms have complementary jobs

Here's how I'm interpreting the architecture.

<box border radius="lg" gap={3} padding={3}>
  <box gap={1}>
    <badge color="info">Mechanism A</badge>
    **Primary crossbar: information capture**
    - Samples the two polar curves.
    - Follows the prescribed motion of their contact points.
    - Carries its own independently rotating elbow.
    - Projects the composite curve onto the tube's inside surface.
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    <badge color="discovery">Mechanism B</badge>
    **Conjugate crossbar: reference and modulation**
    - Samples mirror-flipped contact points.
    - Swings and rotates in the opposite direction.
    - Has its own independent elbow.
    - Carries a pointer arm anchored at the inside rim of the donut hole.
    - Provides a moving reference that cuts through the torus rather than drawing a second composite curve.
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    **Shared element: the sphere**
    Both mechanisms participate in the same sphere's motion, but neither crossbar is physically attached to the other.
  </box>
</box>

The second mechanism could therefore be a kind of *counter-sweeper*: it doesn't duplicate the first mechanism's output; it provides a complementary way of observing and organizing the motion.

## 2. The wobble amplification idea has a mathematical basis

Consider a simplified east-west reflection:

\[
M(x,y,z)=(-x,y,z)
\]

Suppose the first mechanism has a wobble displacement

\[
\mathbf w_1=(w_x,w_y,w_z)
\]

and the second produces its mirror:

\[
\mathbf w_2=M\mathbf w_1
=(-w_x,w_y,w_z).
\]

Now consider their difference:

\[
\mathbf w_1-\mathbf w_2
=(2w_x,0,0).
\]

The east-west antisymmetric component is doubled. The mirror-symmetric components cancel.

That's a particularly interesting result. The two mechanisms could separate the sphere's motion into complementary modes:

- Their difference isolates and amplifies the mirror-antisymmetric wobble.
- Their sum isolates and amplifies the mirror-symmetric motion.

The opposite rotation may reinforce this effect in angular coordinates. If their angular phases are

\[
\theta_1(t)=\omega t,\qquad
\theta_2(t)=-\omega t,
\]

then their relative phase is

\[
\boxed{\Delta\theta(t)=2\omega t}.
\]

So the relative motion completes twice the angular excursion of either mechanism individually.

One qualification: this is an amplification of *relative motion*. If the mechanisms are merely independent tracers, it doesn't physically increase the first crossbar's wobble. If both interact kinematically with the same sphere, however, the sphere provides a shared coupling. That distinction will matter when we formalize the model.

## 3. The second pointer might solve a deeper problem

The pointer arm anchored on the inside rim of the donut hole is especially interesting.

If its motion defines a moving meridional reference through the torus, it gives us another way to describe the location of the primary projected trace.

For a standard ring torus, we can write a point on its surface as

\[
\mathbf T(u,v)=
\begin{pmatrix}
(R+a\cos v)\cos u\\
(R+a\cos v)\sin u\\
a\sin v
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Here:

- \(u\) describes position around the large circumference.
- \(v\) describes position around the tube's cross-section.

The inverse coordinate transformation is

\[
u=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
\]

\[
v=\operatorname{atan2}
\left(z,\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-R\right).
\]

This is useful because the composite curve can then be represented as two functions:

\[
\boxed{C(t)=\big(u(t),v(t)\big)}.
\]

The primary mechanism generates the projected path. The secondary mechanism could provide a moving reference for its toroidal coordinates.

That might make the second mechanism useful not merely for stabilizing or redirecting the projector, but for making the composite curve easier to decode.

## 4. The three information requirements

I think these deserve to be treated as three separate mathematical tests.

| Requirement | What must be true |
|---|---|
| Polar curve reversibility | Each input curve preserves enough information to reconstruct its exact input equation. |
| Composite completeness | The combined trace uniquely represents the simultaneous state of both input curves. |
| Composite reversibility | The torus-surface trace can be converted back into a sufficiently precise equation. |

There is an important subtlety in the first requirement.

A geometric locus alone generally cannot reproduce its exact generating equation. Different parameterizations can describe the same geometric curve. So the object we need is not merely an unlabelled line. It is a **parameterized, oriented, phase-preserving curve**.

The same issue applies to the composite trace. If two different simultaneous states of R and Q project to the same point on the torus, the point alone cannot tell us which state produced it.

The second mechanism may help resolve that ambiguity by supplying another coordinate or reference. But we'll need to demonstrate that rather than assume it.

## 5. Will the second mechanism force closure?

This is the part where I would be cautious.

Mirror symmetry and counterrotation can make the trajectory more orderly, but they do not automatically guarantee finite closure.

For a system with several rotating phases, exact closure requires a common period \(T\) such that

\[
\omega_iT=2\pi n_i
\]

for every independent phase, with integer \(n_i\).

Equivalently, all independent frequency ratios must be rational.

The promising feature of your proposal is that the second mechanism need not introduce an independent clock. If its motions are exact mirror-conjugates of the first mechanism's motions, with reversed phase, then it adds no new independent frequency. It may actually make the combined system easier to phase-lock.

That is where I'd concentrate. We should derive the secondary motion from the primary motion and the reflection operation, rather than give it an independently chosen set of frequencies.

One further detail needs careful treatment: a mirror reflection already reverses handedness. Adding an explicitly opposite rotation can either produce the intended counterrotation or accidentally reverse the sign twice. We'll need to define both angular velocities in the same global coordinate frame.

---

## My current assessment

I see three potentially valuable functions emerging from the second mechanism:

1. **Differential amplification:** it makes certain components of the sphere's wobble more pronounced relative to the first mechanism.
2. **Geometric referencing:** its bagelwise pointer provides an independent moving reference for locating the primary projection on the torus.
3. **Phase regularization:** its mirror-conjugate motion may make the combined system easier to return to a precisely defined initial state.

The third is not yet proven, but it is a plausible design advantage.

I would not change the existing Whirligig implementation yet. The next step should be a mathematical model of both crossbars, their contact-point mappings, their signed rotations, and their shared sphere state. Then we can test three things computationally:

- Whether the secondary mechanism really amplifies the intended wobble modes.
- Whether the primary composite trace retains enough information to reconstruct R and Q.
- Whether the complete system has a finite exact return period.

**The most interesting possibility is that the second mechanism isn't just correcting the first. It may be providing the missing coordinate system that makes the first mechanism's output reversible.**
