I'll build this as a **two-mechanism kinematic prototype**, with the sphere as their shared moving body and no physical connection between the crossbars.

The visualization will show both mechanisms simultaneously:

- **Primary mechanism:** the two polar-curve followers, variable crossbar, midpoint wobble, independent gimbal elbow, and its projected composite trace on the torus's inside tube surface.
- **Conjugate mechanism:** mirror-flipped followers, reversed swing and rotation, its own independent elbow, and the pointer anchored at the donut-hole rim, sweeping its bagelwise plane through the torus.
- **Shared motion:** sphere roll and wobble, with both mechanisms' phases visible so we can inspect whether the combined motion actually closes.

I will keep the specified geometry separate from any provisional choices needed to animate it. In particular, I won't force the second pointer or the first elbow onto a preferred radial half merely to make the picture look orderly.

The first numerical pass gives us an interesting result.

For the existing demonstration inputs,

\[
R(\lambda)=\cos(2\lambda)+\frac{3}{11}\sin(3\lambda)
\]

\[
Q(\lambda)=\sin(3\lambda)+\frac{1}{6}\cos(5\lambda),
\]

I used these phase rules:

\[
\alpha_A=\psi,\qquad \alpha_B=\pi-\psi
\]

\[
\phi_A=+4\psi,\qquad \phi_B=-4\psi.
\]

The secondary pointer's azimuth is provisionally taken from the horizontal projection of its own elbow. That gives it **three complete revolutions around the inner rim per torus orbit**, returning to its starting position. Its horizontal projection does not vanish in the sampled cycle.

A more qualified result: the primary projected trace returns to its starting point after one orbit, with a numerical seam residual of approximately \(1.6\times10^{-14}\). But it is not yet smooth. The full-torus first-intersection branch has 130 adjacent jumps larger than \(0.2b\) in 700 intervals, with a largest jump of about 2.23 model units. The second mechanism gives us a new reference motion; it has not magically cured the first projector's branch changes.

The two midpoint motions also produce a measurable differential wobble. For this demonstration pair, its maximum is \(0.103b\), compared with a maximum individual midpoint offset of \(0.093b\). I'll expose those quantities in the visualization rather than describe the effect as proven amplification.

## What this prototype actually encodes

- **Mechanism A:** the existing R/Q followers, crossbar, midpoint, perpendicular gimbal, and first positive intersection with the *entire* torus surface. The ray solver isolates quartic roots, including tangent roots. It does not restrict the hit to a radial half.
- **Mechanism B:** the R/Q sweep is mirrored with \(\alpha_B=\pi-\psi\), and its own elbow rotates with phase \(-4\psi\). Its horizontal azimuth determines the position of the inner-rim pointer anchor. That pointer defines the radial BigRad line and meridional slice.
- **The sphere:** retains the equal-area Analemma and the common two-circuit sphere-roll/material phase. The crossbars have no linkage to each other.
- **The body view:** displays R, Q, the Analemma, and both follower chords. The main view displays the actual torus projection and the second mechanism's slice.

The three information requirements are not all proven yet. The follower parameters \(t_R,t_Q\) are retained alongside the trace, and each projected point is converted to torus coordinates \((u,v)\). That gives us the data needed to investigate reconstruction. But the composite curve alone has not yet been shown to uniquely determine both input equations. The second pointer may supply the missing phase reference: the next mathematical test is whether the augmented record \((u,v,\theta_B)\) lets us recover the corresponding input parameters without ambiguity.

The app uses the current demonstration equations, not arbitrary user-supplied equations. No repository files were changed; this is an in-thread prototype based on the [current Whirligig mechanism](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/PUBLIC_SITE/instruments/whirligig/index.html) and the [original 3D construction](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/db32abc75a4a2cff3afc6de895cd7edb9eb62d82/_AUTO_EXTRACTED_TEXT/FINDING%20THE%20DONUT%20(nolat).txt).

**One detail to settle before refining the mechanics:** is the second pointer arm meant to use the horizontal azimuth of its own elbow to locate its anchor on the inner rim, as this prototype does? <MemoryCite />
